title: Muslim women's voices
hookLine: Muslim women speak for themselves on dress, work, scholarship and faith, and they don't all agree

cards: A woman comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a complaint about her husband.
He has spoken an old pagan formula over her, and by the custom of the time it means she is cut off from him, neither married nor free. She argues her case. She doesn't let it drop.
She turns her complaint to Allah. And the surah that opens with her story is named for her argument: al-Mujadila, she who disputes.
Its first verse says that Allah has heard the woman who pleaded with the Prophet about her husband. Her name, tradition says, was Khawlah.

teach.b: Tradition says Umm Salamah, the Prophet's wife, asked why the Qur'an spoke of men and not of women, and that a verse in surah al-Ahzab came down naming both, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe".
And 'A'ishah became a teacher whom companions consulted. In Sahih Muslim, she praises the women of the Ansar, saying, in paraphrase, that shyness didn't keep them from learning their religion.
Tradition also remembers women who narrated hadith and taught it, with men among their students, and that line of women teaching continues in schools and mosques today.
Today's voices come in the plural.
Muslim women write on law, run clinics, lead businesses, raise families, recite the Qur'an, preach to women's gatherings, and argue in public, on dress, work, mosque space and scholarship.
And they don't all agree. Some argue from the classical schools. Some propose fresh readings of the texts.
Some wear hijab and some don't, and both explain their reasons. Some work outside the home and some choose not to, and give their reasons too.
These disagreements happen among Muslim women themselves; nobody needs an outsider, or a narrator, to settle them. What a listener can do is notice who is speaking. A Muslim woman, in her own words?

how: Muslim women teach in mosques and schools, narrate and study hadith, write and speak on law and faith, and lead women's study circles; they hold a range of views on dress, work and mosque space, and argue for them in their own words.

practice: Let the sounds around you come and go without naming them, a car, a fan, your own breath, and for a few breaths just receive, the way the surah begins: someone spoke, and was heard.
If you pray, ask in your own words for a hearing heart.

wordCard.voice: Muslim women's voices. From Khawlah and 'A'ishah to scholars and writers today, women speaking for themselves on faith, dress, work and learning, and not always agreeing. Today's word.
